summary: L-4 cab bolted to a rock spire in the Boulder River Wilderness, staffed in the 1930s-40s, abandoned, restored in 1986, and now volunteer-maintained.

facts.status_note: Restored in 1986 by volunteers after abandonment; roof and other repairs redone in 2015. Not rented; maintained by The Mountaineers.

access.note: In the Boulder River Wilderness; reachable by a long, exposed hike/scramble, no road access.

visit.trail_note: ~16 miles round trip, ~5,000 ft gain, most hikers take two days; final approach involves scrambling.

events.note: Engles and Bedal scouted the peak as a lookout site.
NHLR gives 1931 as the build/first-staffed year; Wikipedia/NRHP give construction spanning 1930-1932.
Wikipedia/NRHP: construction completed over a three-year period, 1930 to 1932, by Harold Engles and Fred Benesh.
Wikipedia/NRHP: staffed seasonally 1933-1942, then abandoned for financial reasons.
NHLR: staffed for ten years and abandoned in 1943.
Restoration led by the daughter of the last observer, completed in 1986.
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, reference 87001190.
NHLR date registered: July 15, 1993; also the year retired Ranger Engles died, having seen the restoration completed.
Roof replaced with cedar shingles, windows repaired, and cab repainted by Mountaineers volunteers, materials flown in by Snohomish County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

evidence.supports: Engles and Bedel picked the site in 1931 (NHLR date); materials hauled by windlass; staffed 10 years, abandoned 1943; restored 1986 by last observer's daughter; Engles died Aug 1993.
evidence.quote: Although the Three Fingers Lookout was staffed for only ten years and abandoned in 1943, the daughter of the last observer led the project to restore the 14 x 14 L-4 groundhouse in 1986.

evidence.supports: Retired Ranger Engles encouraged efforts to save the lookout and lived to see the restoration completed before he died in August 1993.
evidence.quote: Efforts to keep the building were encouraged by retired Ranger Engles who lived to see the project completed before his passing in August, 1993.

evidence.supports: Built 1930-1932 by Engles and Benesh; staffed 1933-1942 then abandoned for financial reasons; listed NRHP 1987; L-4 design lacking catwalk due to site.
evidence.quote: The building was staffed seasonally between 1933 and 1942, and was then abandoned for financial reasons. Everett Mountaineers, a local mountaineering group, has taken over its maintenance.

evidence.supports: Construction details: blasted 15 ft off pinnacle, materials packed to within 600 ft then tram/ropes/ladders; L-4 lacking catwalk; Engles and Bedal scaled the peak in 1929 to assess feasibility, construction 1930-1932.
evidence.quote: The lookout was built over a three-year period between 1930 and 1932 by Harold Engles and Fred Benesh. Engles and Harry Bedal had first scaled the peak in 1929, to investigate its feasibility as a fire observation site, given its visual prominence. The site was prepared by blasting 15 feet (4.6 m) off the top of the pinnacle to create a level foundation. Construction materials were brought by pack animals to within 600 feet (180 m) of the summit, and transported via a tram system to the work site, which was accessed by a series of ropes and ladders. The building is a nearly standard example of an L-4 Forest Service lookout, lacking only an outside catwalk due to the site geography.

evidence.supports: 2015 roof replacement with cedar shingles by Mountaineers volunteers; helicopter delivery of materials allowed after Forest Service review; hike is ~16 miles, ~5,000 ft gain, two days for most hikers.
evidence.quote: Just getting there is a challenge — about 16 miles and 5,000 feet of gain. Most hikers need two days.

evidence.supports: Helicopter normally not allowed in wilderness but permitted here after a minimum requirements analysis; materials delivered by cargo net.
evidence.quote: Normally, a helicopter drop would not be allowed at the lookout because it is within the wilderness area. But the U.S. Forest Service decided the use of a helicopter was the best way to do it.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR says built/staffed starting 1931, abandoned 1943 (10 years staffed). Wikipedia/NRHP nomination says built 1930-1932, staffed 1933-1942. Both ranges are given in the story rather than picking one.

sources.title: Three Fingers fire lookout has a new roof, thanks to brave volunteers
sources.publisher: The Herald (Everett, WA), via National Historic Lookout Register

notes_for_editor: Build/staffing date ranges genuinely conflict between NHLR and the NRHP nomination (via Wikipedia); kept both in the story rather than resolving. Current record's 'built 1931' and 'abandoned 1942' event years fall within these ranges and are not contradicted, so no correction filed.
